purpose: Lurasidone is used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar depression in adults and some children and teenagers. It helps reduce symptoms like hallucinations, disorganized thinking, and feelings of depression associated with bipolar disorder. Your doctor may also use it for other conditions not listed here.
how_it_works: Lurasidone works by balancing certain natural chemicals in your brain, especially dopamine and serotonin. When these chemicals are out of balance, they can cause symptoms like hearing voices, paranoia, or severe mood swings. By helping rebalance these brain chemicals, lurasidone helps you think more clearly and feel more stable emotionally.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include drowsiness or sleepiness, restlessness or an urge to keep moving (called akathisia), nausea, slow or stiff movements, and weight gain. Some people may also notice dizziness, especially when standing up quickly. Most side effects are manageable and may get better over time.
warnings: This medication can increase the risk of high blood sugar and diabetes, so tell your doctor if you have diabetes or a family history of it. It can also cause a rare but serious movement disorder called tardive dyskinesia. Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis should not take this drug as it can increase the risk of death. Do not drink grapefruit juice while taking this medication, as it can increase the drug level in your body. Always tell your doctor about all medications you take, as many drugs can interact with lurasidone.
typical_dosing: Lurasidone is taken once a day by mouth, always with a meal of at least 350 calories — this is very important because food helps your body absorb the medication properly. The starting dose is usually 40 mg per day, and your doctor may gradually increase it based on how you respond, up to a maximum of 160 mg per day. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
